en: The Ritual for Cultivation and Realization Based on the Abridged Text of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* Compiled by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui Part One:
General Introduction to the Origins Part Two: Adorning and Purifying the Practice Hall (Dochang)
Third, the Invocation of the Sages; Fourth, the Contemplative Gate of Making Offerings;
Fifth, Right Seating and Reflection; Sixth, Praising the Tathāgata;
Seventh, Paying Homage to the Triple Gem; Eighth, Practicing the Five Repentances.

Regarding the ninth, the circumambulation and recitation, and the tenth, the exhortation through admonition, as well as the various family liturgies for repentance (*li-chan*), one first makes offerings of incense and flowers. As for the preliminary invocation performed here first, the *Guang-yi* (Extensive Ritual) states:
If one does not first extend an invitation, whom would one wish to provide offerings for? It is certainly appropriate to invite them first; there is a profound significance in this.
First, a general account of the origin:

when our Buddha proclaimed the *Complete Enlightenment* (*Yuanjue*), he opened the Dharma of the One Mind to encompass those of the three capacities. This was indeed because of [the presence of] hindrances...

There are degrees of depth in this, corresponding to the sharpness or dullness of one's spiritual capacity (*indriya*). For this reason, the general and specific methods of contemplation are distinguished as two separate gates.

The repentance at the site of practice (*dojang*) follows as the third; it is like a fine horse already shaking off the shadow of the whip, or like a great treasure buried in the dust that requires the application of a remedial method.
Now, regarding the meaning of repentance (*chan*), there is both repentance in principle (*li-chan*) and repentance in action (*shi-chan*).
As for this: to lay bare one’s transgressions with diligent effort, to reproach the deluded mind with profound remorse—this is the ritual of repentance (*sāṃghāṭī*).

To contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) with tranquil composure, and to let the sun of wisdom shine upon the frost and dew—this is the principle of repentance. Since the Han and Wei dynasties, this method of repentance has been revered, yet it is rarely heard that anyone has truly mastered it.
This is surely because the source of the teaching had only recently begun to flow and the sūtras and śāstras were not yet complete (referring to the various Vaipulya sūtras).
In treatises such as the *Vibhāṣā*, the Dharma Master Mitian of the Western Jin dynasty once composed the *Four Seasons Liturgical Texts*.

Observing the words of his solemn offerings and the fivefold repentance, one sees that he honored the scriptures and esteemed their meaning, extracting much of their essential points; thus, scholars throughout the land took pleasure in and practiced them.

During the transition between the Chen and Sui dynasties, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi compiled the *Dharma Flower Repentance Method*, and its various aspects—both those in accord with and contrary to the path—are fully manifested in the *Guanming Baolu*.
The "Ten Minds" (Shixin) is a ritual manual that is quite detailed and has been widely practiced in the region south of the Yangtze River.

During the Middle Tang period, our ancestor, Master Guifeng, followed in the illustrious footsteps of Nanyue Huisi and carried forward the legacy of Zhiyi. He composed an exhaustive exposition on the *Complete Enlightenment Liturgy for Repentance and Meditation* in eighteen fascicles.
Because it encompasses exhortations for practice and provides a systematic account of the signs of realization, it serves as the liturgical framework for the rites performed within the Dharma-hall.
The gates [of this ritual] consist of seven, whereas the gates of the *Lifó chányí* (Ritual for Bowing to the Buddha and Repentance) consist of eight.

That which is therein set forth and cited is profound, subtle, vast, and extensive—drawing largely upon the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and other such works—and it essentially concerns the cultivation and realization achieved within the three periods of time.

Having encountered these bequeathed instructions at the end of the Semblance Dharma age, I have contemplated the Pure Practices for many years. Consequently, I have abridged this from its extensive original version.
For this reason, I have composed this separate work. Its principles and categories follow one another, filling the entirety of this single scroll.

Now, observing that its phrasing, though different from [the teachings of] Miti (Tiantai), and its resonance, seem to harmonize with those of Zhizhe (Zhiyi)—both Tianzhu and Ximing being descendants of the lineage of Zhizhe—if later students of the final age continue to cultivate these teachings, then the merit of Guifeng’s diligent labors will have been repaid even in a ten-thousandth part.

Second, Adorning and Purifying the Site of Enlightenment (This section corresponds to the sixth part of the ritual procedures for the site of enlightenment; it is now recorded separately as a summary of the essential points of the abbreviated version).

Now, clothing and the physical body are both the bases upon which the mind of a practitioner relies. If one wishes to cultivate this Perfect and Sudden Great Practice, one must first employ the method of prostration and repentance;
this requires a pure mind. Since the mind does not arise in isolation, it must necessarily rely upon conditions and objects.
Because the objects of perception are pure, the mind is likewise pure; therefore, one must strictly purify these three matters.

Furthermore, if one wishes to invoke the worthy sages, the altar site must be strictly purified. If the altar site is not solemn and clean, the aspiration for the Way will not arise, and there will be no response or descent of the divine.
For this reason, one should adorn the altar, purify one's garments, and bathe the body; one must abandon all trivial affairs and bring both body and mind under control.

Make offerings to the Triple Gem. With single-minded devotion, bring to mind all evil karma committed since we first acquired this body, as well as all such karma from past lives, and repent with focused diligence.
May our bodies and minds be purified when practicing contemplation, so that all our aspirations and requests may be fully realized.
Regarding the method for the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), one must first select a location that is free from clamor, distraction, impurity, and filth.
Regarding various obstacles and difficulties: if one finds a deep, secluded mountain valley or a remote forest spring that is most exceptionally wondrous, it is ideal.

If one is in a human settlement, one must remove one or two chi of the old earth and smear the ground with fragrant mud. Hang various banners and flowers, and place an image of Rocana Buddha in the center of the hall.
On both sides, place images of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; these constitute the Three Holy Ones. Before the Buddha [place...]

Place the *Anuttara-bodhi-maṇḍala-sūtra* (The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment) in a case to store it. Light lotus lamps and burn incense of a hundred ingredients. As for the various articles of adornment, they need only be pure;
they need not be fine or expensive. Each should act according to their means; however, when one’s effort reaches its limit, that itself constitutes the most precious offering.

These are originally offered to the worthy sages and saints solely to manifest one’s own sincere devotion. How could the worthy sages have likes or dislikes? (The two characters "likes" and "dislikes"...)
[All terms are pronounced with the departing tone]. As for the method of arrangement, it may be done according to one’s own convenience; there is no fixed ritual.

Next, regarding the purification of clothing: although an ordained person ought inherently to maintain purity, if one has generally failed to observe this vigilance, then upon entering the *maṇḍala*, one must wear new, clean garments (if no new ones are available, wash old ones). Furthermore, one must bathe the body. If the body...
How could one who is defiled by impure contact ever approach the sages and worthies? Although the Buddhas have no [discriminating] mind, the spirits and deities do not protect them;

when the spirits and deities do not protect them, malevolent spirits and demons will cause agitation and create obstacles and hindrances. It is not enough merely to purify the body; one must especially purify the mind.

By severing all discursive thoughts, even if one encounters obstacles and hindrances, there shall be no retreat from one's resolve. Only when the three karmas are pure may one enter the place of practice (*maṇḍala*). Upon first entering...

One should observe the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*). On these days, the messengers of the Four Heavenly Kings and the great benevolent deities descend to the human realm to inspect good and evil.
Upon seeing a practitioner, they offer consolation and protection, manifesting auspicious signs to cause the practitioner’s heart to rejoice and to augment their faculties.
(From here below, the eight sections follow the sequence of the *Guangxiuzhengyi* [Extensive Ritual for Cultivation and Realization]).
Third, the Invocation:

When one desires to arouse the bodhicitta to wash away the defilements of sin, and applies diligent effort to enter the wondrous realm, one should at all times pray that all the worthy sages and holy ones of the ten directions act as witnesses.
Although the Buddhas and worthy sages are omnipresent, if one does not remain reverent...

Please understand that although [the Buddha] is present, he does not manifest [in a fixed form]; therefore, one must rely upon wisdom. Even when recognizing him, one should always maintain the perception of the Buddha;
with a pure mind and luminous wisdom, the principle adapts to changing phenomena, and one thus constantly sees the Buddha—this is called "pure dependent origination. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"For example, when the sun rises and shines universally upon the world, its reflection appears without exception in all vessels of clear water. The Buddha-sun is likewise; it manifests everywhere."
The Dharma-realm has neither beginning nor end; within the water-vessels of the pure minds of all sentient beings, there is no Buddha who does not manifest.

Nevertheless, when the practitioner first enters the ritual arena, they should recite the name of Vairocana Buddha. Circumambulating once to the right, they proceed to the Dharma-seat, where they spread their *niṣīdana* mat.
With body upright and mindfulness correct, they must carefully avoid distraction. Joining their palms, they stand waiting. The one of venerable virtue then leads the chant.
[The Master] says:
"With all reverence, with single-minded devotion, we prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions.

(This is a general prostration to the Triple Gem; kneeling on one knee with hands clasped around the incense burner, burn various famous incenses to show respect to the sages and worthies. This is performed only at the three daily invitations; it is not used at other times.)

With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Buddha Vairocana, the Great Luminous Treasury, the Source of both Ordinary and Holy Beings, who manifests all Pure Lands, and whose Dharma-body and Reward-body are perfectly integrated.
(Recite this three times and perform one prostration; all subsequent invocations shall follow this pattern.)
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat Śākyamuni Buddha of the Sahā World,
as well as the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who together proclaim the Perfect Enlightenment in that Pure Land.

With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time: those who abide in the ground of pure enlightenment, who are adorned with light, who maintain their vows until the end of the future, and who protect the Perfect Enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in the Great Vaipulya Sūtra on Perfect Enlightenment, the definitive meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
the pure eye of all teachings, the profound treasury of the Mahāyāna of sudden instruction.

With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the Greatly Wise Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and the Greatly Practicing Samantabhadra Bodhisattva Mahāsattva within the Assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiance Treasury.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Vidyutprabha, Samantacakṣu,
Vajragarbha, Maitreya, and Viśuddhamati from within the Assembly of the Pure Land.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the Mahāsattvas:
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Viśvabhūṣaṇa Bodhisattva, Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśuddhi Bodhisattva, and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, who are specifically elucidated within the assembly of the Pure Land.
With single-minded devotion, we invoke the presence of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra (Worthy Leader of the Virtuous),

together with his retinue of one hundred thousand Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, who presides over the site of practice within the assembly of the Pure Land and propagates the teachings of the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat Namah to the Greatly Compassionate Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the patriarchs Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna,
and all the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and noble saṃgha of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

With single-minded devotion, we invoke: the protectors of the Dharma within the assembly of the Pure Land, including Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, as well as Agniśikha-vajra and the Great Powerful Ghost-King with all their retinues;

furthermore, the spirits of the famous mountains and great rivers within this nation, the deities of the specific province and its jurisdiction, and those who guard the monastery where we currently reside.
The Blue Deity who Upholds the True Dharma and all the worthy sages (from "guarding" downwards, there are only three requests; one should not prostrate. For laypeople, there is no prohibition).
The Fourth: The Contemplation Gate of Offering. (Having completed the invocation, we know that all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas do not disregard our request.

From the Great Treasury of Radiance, the Assembly of the Equal Dharma, they respond to our invocation through the power of their samādhi and compassion, appearing before us without moving from their state. Although our fleshly eyes cannot see them, by concentrating our minds in contemplation, we perceive them with perfect clarity.

We see Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and various worthies and sages filling the site of enlightenment and pervading the realm of empty space. Knowing and seeing our sincere and earnest invocation, we should therefore offer incense and flowers. Holding the censers, chant as follows:)
All these assemblies, each kneeling in turn, solemnly holding incense and flowers to make offerings according to the Dharma, cease their chanting at this point.
Holding the flowers with their hands, they should silently recite while forming this visualization: "The pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas."
The merit is immeasurable; it neither abides nor perishes. It is serene and eternally peaceful.
The incense and flowers I grasp are all produced from grasses and trees. I offer them to all Buddhas, maintaining this visualization as my offering.
From every pore of my body, may countless incense and flowers emerge, one from each pore, to offer to all Buddhas and transform into [a vast array].
The fragrant flower-altars, having been accepted by the Buddhas, perform Buddha-works throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
they then return and become golden altars, remaining before us. Having visualized this, recite:
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the worlds of the ten directions, Making offerings to all Buddhas, the Honored Dharma,
and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. May they accept these clouds of incense and flowers as luminous towers,
Extending throughout boundless realms, performing immeasurable Buddha-deeds.

The above is all based on the intent of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*. Furthermore, the eighteen lines of verse in the preceding commentary are also from the prose section (*gadya*) of that same sutra;
I have here merely extracted the essential meaning and versified it so that practitioners may silently recite and contemplate them without omission.
Moreover, many silk and colored flower offerings are presented within the *maṇḍala*, as these serve as substitutes for frost and snow.
At this time, there are no flowers of grass or trees; at other times, one seeks them according to the sutras and offers them to the Triple Gem.

Having made the offering, everyone should rise with full reverence and perform one prostration. (The *Guangyi* states: "Offerings eliminate the obstacles of stinginess and greed accumulated over many kalpas, so that in every lifetime one attains great wealth.")
Fifth, one should sit upright and contemplate this single gateway.
According to the *Guangchanhui* (Extensive Repentance), the method for clear sitting meditation consists of seven gateways following the practice of circumambulation.

Within these, one regulates the body and clarifies the mind, cultivating *śamatha* (calm abiding) and giving rise to *vipaśyanā* (insight). These are distinguished individually according to the various gateways as one encounters conditions and objects. Now:
The seven luminaries are suspended in the Great Clarity (*taiqing*), so that all things may behold them.

Now, when a practitioner cultivates a single session, they stand facing the Dharma-seat in a level position, sitting upright with the body straight, binding their mindfulness to the counting of breaths.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "If sentient beings cultivate *dhyāna*, they first take up the counting [of breaths]."

[The] Gate. The Commentary states: "This has two meanings. First, one first employs the gate of breath-counting meditation (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) to subdue various discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*), gradually entering the wondrous state.
Second, as the subsequent sutra says: 'In the mind, one clearly knows the arising, abiding, and ceasing of thoughts, along with their boundaries and counts. The Explanation states:
This merely clarifies the skillful means for cultivating the Middle Way of absolute non-referentiality (*atyanta-nirapekṣa-madhyamā-pratipad*). Thus, it is known that [this is] absolute..."
Only through the wisdom of mindfulness can one fully comprehend the arising, abiding, and ceasing of thoughts. Therefore, following this gate of contemplation, one should further understand:
to discern the coarse and the subtle; to remain at all times without giving rise to deluded thoughts; yet not to immediately extinguish the various deluded minds;
to dwell within the realm of delusive thought such that it cannot be fully comprehended; and, in the absence of such comprehension, not to discriminate between the real and the unreal.
Indeed, to speak of it directly, this is its wondrousness. Having offered worship and reflection upon the Tathāgata as described in the sixth chapter on Praise,
one should then immediately straighten the body and demeanor, stand attentively with a single mind, and join in praising all [the Buddhas].

Regarding the Buddha’s subtle and wondrous merits, the *Guangyi* (Extensive Commentary) states: "By chanting and praising [this name], one eliminates the obstacles of abusive speech and so forth accumulated over immeasurable kalpas and attains the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
His physical form is golden light, pure and stainless; his eyes are like clear, deep-blue lapis lazuli."
The auspicious majesty of his renown is heard everywhere; The sun of great compassion and wisdom dispels the darkness of the multitude.
The moon of the Muni shines with ultimate coolness, Able to remove the fever of afflictions for sentient beings.
His inconceivable merit is peerless, Like the atoms of all buddha-fields, beyond counting.

The wisdom of our Buddha is likewise; all sentient beings cannot know it, even if they contemplate it with earnest thought for immeasurable eons, for no one can fathom the ocean of his merit and wisdom.
Having offered this praise, I shall now describe the intent behind establishing this repentance, as set forth according to the capacity of my own intellectual power, and so forth.
Seventh, having completed the praise and veneration of the Triple Gem,
one should single-mindedly pay homage in successive order. Regarding the method for prostrating to the Buddha, one must,
in accordance with the particular Buddha being venerated, mindfully recollect that this Buddha’s true body is like empty space, manifesting in response to sentient beings.
The forms [of the Buddhas] appear as if before one's eyes; they receive my prostrations. Furthermore, one must know for oneself that body and mind are empty and still, devoid of any marks of worship.
According to pure conditions, reflections manifest within the Dharma-realm; before each and every Buddha, this very body is present.

The Tripitaka Master Ratnamati explained seven types of prostration with their specific protocols, as found in the *Lengyan Xiu Zheng Yi* (Ritual for Cultivation and Realization of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra).
Discriminate this: do not perform prostrations with a mind of arising and ceasing. Thus, the *Guangyi* (Extensive Ritual) states:
"Sincere and reverent prostration can eliminate the obstacles of pride accumulated over immeasurable kalpas, whereby one attains a noble and honorable body."

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to Vairocana Buddha, the Great Treasury of Radiance, the source of all Buddhas and sentient beings, who manifests all pure lands to respond to the capacities of those with perfect faculties.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to our original teacher Śākyamuni, who appears as hundreds and thousands of transformation bodies throughout the Sahā world to respond to the capacities of beings.
Muni Buddha,
with single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Great Luminous Treasury, the ground of pure awakening for all sentient beings, the radiant adornment and sustainer of all Buddhas.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whose physical forms are interpenetrating and whose speech is unimpeded, all of whom preach the Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra-vijñāna). With single-minded devotion,
I pay homage to those of great kindness and great compassion who, through their great vows, shall protect the Perfect Enlightenment until the end of the future.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time,
with one mind, pay homage to the Great Vaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment, the definitive meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
the pure eye, the profound treasury of the Dharma of the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, who, within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Luminous Treasury, has developed the causal ground and manifested the wisdom of faith, understanding, and realization.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, who, within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiance Treasury, elucidates the illusory nature of phenomena and manifests the principles and practices of compassionate vows.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to him who, within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiance Treasury, perceives all phenomena as entirely pure and universally manifest.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva single-mindedly prostrated to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, who, within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Luminous Matrix, decisively resolves profound doubts.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, who profoundly investigates the root of saṃsāra within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiance Treasury.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the one who clearly penetrates the stages of cultivation and realization within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiance Treasury.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prajñā,

with single-minded devotion, prostrated himself before the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vidyutprabha-vaśitā, who had manifested the three kinds of wondrous contemplations within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiance Treasury.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vidyutkumāra (Discerning Sound), who manifests the twenty-five wheels within the assembly of the Great Radiant Treasury Pure Land.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to [the one] who, within the assembly of the Great Radiant Treasury Pure Land, gives rise to the awakened mind by eliminating the four marks.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions,

with single-minded devotion, prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Awakening, who had requested instruction from the Teacher within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiant Treasury, in order to eliminate the four illnesses.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Perfect Enlightenment, who initiated the practice hall within the Assembly of the Pure Land of Great Radiance and realized the principle of the ultimate awakening.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to those within the Assembly of the Pure Land of Great Radiance who propagate the teachings to extensively save future generations.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhadramukha,
with single-minded devotion, prostrated himself before the assembly in the Pure Land of the Great Radiant Treasury, together with his retinue of one hundred thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion, the patriarchs Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna,
and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— both those still in training and those beyond training— the assembly of worthy and holy ones throughout the dust-mote worlds within the entirety of space across the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Eighth, regarding the practice of the five repentances:
having completed the prostrations to the Buddhas, one should maintain upright posture and dignified demeanor.

With reverent devotion, kneel with the right knee touching the ground and burn various famous incenses while visualizing the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra surrounded by his immeasurable, magnificently adorned retinue.

Circumambulate [the image]. Acting as the presiding master of repentance, as if facing them before one's eyes, with single-minded devotion and profound shame, confess and reveal all evil karma created through the six sense organs and three types of action throughout immeasurable kalpas, severing the continuity of such thoughts.
From this moment until the end of the future, I shall never again commit such acts. Why is this? Although the nature of karma is empty, its retribution is not lost.
Therefore, the practitioner confesses and reveals their transgressions, vowing that their sins may be extinguished. The *Guangyi* (Broad Ritual) states:
"Confession universally removes the three obstructions, resulting in the fulfillment of both the primary and secondary rewards. One should single-mindedly reflect, saying:
For all the karmic obstacles of sin committed by myself and all sentient beings since beginningless time, I pray that the Triple Gem will compassionately deliver us.
May our deluded karma be instantly dispelled and transformed into pure causes; may body and mind together become empty, such that neither sin nor merit has a master.

May we clearly perceive the true nature, which is equal to the Buddha’s Dharmakāya, and may the transgressions of the three karmas become the three gates of liberation. May the heavy obstructions of the six sense faculties be overturned...
Perform the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Next, chant:
"Universally for the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu*, may all obstacles be severed; I take refuge and repent.
Having finished chanting, rise and perform one prostration, while cultivating the ten minds of contrariness and compliance.
Furthermore, one should recollect the *Śītalā-gāthā*, which says:
"Since beginningless time, I have given rise to ignorance; I have also encountered evil friends, increasing my afflictions.
Lacking a mind of sympathetic joy, my virtue has been forever extinguished, And within myself, verbal and mental evils have gradually arisen."
Mind upon mind, pervasive and stained by contact; Thought after thought, continuous, busying day and night, Seeking not to be known by others, concealing one's transgressions;
Fearless of the evil realms, acting with total license, Lacking shame and dread of blame—the net of Māra— Denying cause and denying effect—the pit of icchantikas.
Thus, having followed the current and turned one's back on the source, the ocean of birth-and-death suffering has become vast and overflowing.
Fortunately, you are a son of a noble family who knows its origin; now you wish to go against the current and abandon the poor village.
With right faith in cause and effect, you destroy the icchantikas; with shame and remorse, you transcend both humans and devas and shatter ignorance.
Fearing the evil realms destroys fearlessness; Confessing sinful karma destroys concealment;
Severing the mind of continuity destroys constant recollection; Arousing the bodhicitta destroys pervasive arising;
Cultivating merit to compensate for faults destroys indulgence; Guarding the true Dharma destroys lack of joy.
"Recalling the Buddhas of the ten directions to destroy evil friends; contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses to destroy the fetters.

These six verses above—of which the first three accord with the mind of birth and death as that which is to be remedied, and the latter three oppose the mind of birth and death by overturning it from the end—should be recited and silently contemplated thoroughly. Next, speak these words:
I, Bhikṣu [Name], with a sincere heart, repent. I bow my head and take refuge in the inexhaustible Triple Gem of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

May you bear witness, protect, and keep me in mind. From beginningless, vast kalpas ago, I and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm have had our minds shrouded by ignorance, losing ourselves in the wisdom of our own Buddha-nature.
Driven by deluded consciousness, we have created karma and revolved in the cycle of birth and death, turning our backs on the Buddha.
The Dharma and the Sangha follow evil teachers and friends. The faculty of the eye, attached to forms, becomes a slave to craving and affection;

thus one fails to behold the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, which is all-pervasive. The ear greedily craves the realm of sounds, leading to endless harm; thus one does not hear the Tathāgata’s perfect voice preaching the Dharma.

The nose greedily craves fragrant scents, whereby the fetters and latent tendencies arise; thus one cannot perceive or savor the wondrous fragrance of merit. The tongue greedily craves various flavors, devouring them...

Sentient beings engage in false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh words; they slander the Triple Gem and insult their parents. How could they partake of the profound flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma?
Their faculty of the body clings to touch with endless attachment and defilement; day and night they remain mired in confusion, knowing no contentment.
They commit all manner of evil deeds—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and thus the compassionate light of the Buddhas cannot illuminate them. Their faculty of the mind...

Attached to dharmas, they grasp at sensory objects and conditions; in every thought-moment, greed, anger, and false views constantly arise. They fully commit all karmas of the three obstacles and perform every kind of transgression.

The three obstacles and the ten entanglements pull one another along without interruption; giving rise to the four inversions, they become icchantikas. Disrespecting their elders and kin, they lack both shame and remorse.
They personally commit, teach others to commit, and approve of seeing the ten evil deeds, the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and the seven prohibitions.
I rejoice. When a single delusion arises, a million obstacles open up; thus, in an endless succession, all manner of obstacles to the various wholesome dharmas are prepared.
One cannot give rise to the mind of great bodhi, nor can one practice any wholesome dharma. One suffers through the long night without ever feeling weary of it.
Such transgressions as these are known only to the Buddha’s awakening; I now repent them all, severing the continuity of such thoughts. How much more so...
These karmic obstructions arise solely from inversion; they possess no fixed reality and are fundamentally empty and quiescent.
We pray that the Sun of Wisdom of Vairocana Buddha and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva will shed their radiant light to melt away the frost and dew of the delusions and karma within our bodies and minds.

May the breeze of compassion blow universally to shatter the mountains of heavy obstructions, and may the waters of the Dharma flow eternally to wash away the defilements of our hearts. We pray only that the roots of our transgressions may be extinguished.
Extinction. One swiftly attains the fundamental mind, and all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm equally attain purity.
Having completed the repentance, one takes refuge and pays homage to Rocana Buddha and the Triple Gem in their entirety.
(The remaining four dharmas all rely upon this; they differ only in that "exhortation" and so forth are substituted for [the previous term]).

Regarding the ritual of exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*): [The *Vistara-vidhi* states: "Exhortation removes the obstacle of slandering the Dharma over many eons, and ensures that in every birth one obtains great learning and eloquence."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], with a sincere heart, entreat you:
To the Tamer of the World who has first attained the Way in the ten directions, I reverently beseech you to turn the Wheel of Dharma out of compassion.
If there are Tathāgatas who wish to enter parinirvāṇa, May they remain in the world forever for the sake of all sentient beings.
The Method of Rejoicing (The Extensive Ritual states: Rejoicing eliminates the obstacles of jealousy accumulated over many kalpas; in every birth, one obtains a vast retinue of spiritual friends).
I, the bhikṣu [so-and-so], rejoice with a sincere heart.
All the roots of goodness cultivated by the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, by bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and ordinary beings— I rejoice in them all with full accord.
The Method of Dedication (The Extensive Ritual states: "Dedication removes narrow and inferior obstacles and accomplishes vast goodness").
I, the bhikṣu [Name], dedicate with a sincere heart.
Since we first turned toward the Buddha, all the causes and conditions of merit we have cultivated are dedicated toward Great Bodhi;
may they be universally shared with all sentient beings so that they may realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
[The *Guǎngyí* says: "Making this vow removes the obstacle of despondency; it enables one to eliminate all obstacles to the *dhāraṇī* and swiftly reach the wondrous fruit."]
I, Bhikṣu [Name], make this vow with a sincere heart:
May I repent and eliminate all karmic obstacles; May my mind open and my intellect be liberated, penetrating the source of spiritual wisdom;
When the six consciousnesses function, may they proceed with right wisdom; Wherever the six sense-objects appear, may the true emptiness manifest.

Ninth: Circumambulating with Mindfulness of the Buddha (Having finished the confession and making the vow, one should single-mindedly circumambulate the Dharma seat to the right, burning various incenses and walking slowly and calmly while reciting the names of the Triple Gem).
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Homage to the Dharma of the ten directions. Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions.
Homage to the Perfectly Harmonious Teacher, Vairocana Buddha. Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha, who responds to conditions according to capacity.
Homage to all Buddhas who maintain the Radiant Adornment. Homage to the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who together proclaim Perfect Enlightenment.
Homage to all Buddhas of the three periods of time who protect Perfect Enlightenment.
Homage to the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment.
Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Homage to the hundred thousand bodhisattvas, beginning with Samantacakṣus;
homage to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ten directions.
As for those who circumambulate, they do so out of longing and devotion for the subtle and wondrous merits of the Triple Gem. Thus, three times, and so forth...

Seven hundred and seven circumambulations are likewise not fixed in number. Next, recite the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment. Regarding the chanting of this text, Master Shengde stated:
"The Dharma-Gate of Cultivation and Realization in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*. As for the formal protocol for reciting the sūtra:

The details are as distinguished in the *Pranidhāna-vidhi* (Ritual of Vows). Once the recitation of the sutra is completed, one should proceed before the Buddha with single-minded right mindfulness, chant the Three Refuges, and exit by circling to the right.

Tenth: Exhortation to Practice through Admonition (In the extensive version, the exhortation to practice appears at the beginning; here, for the sake of this abbreviated version, the intention of the admonition is stated first, and therefore it is placed at the end).
According to this sutra, if a long-term period is established, it shall be one hundred and twenty days; a medium-term period, one hundred days; and a short-term period, eighty days.
Since the ten superior gates have already been recorded in detail as a separate ritual manual, it is appropriate to take seven days as a single period of time.

This may continue for up to seven weeks, as long as one is able to do so according to one's inclination. Day and night, during the six periods, one should pay homage and make supplications to the Triple Gem.
One must not make excuses for negligence or indulge in sleep, nor should one harbor thoughts of the five worldly desires for even a moment.

Whether one practices on the third, eighth, or fifteenth days of the month, or performs it every day, there is no fixed requirement. However, if one does so at the beginning of the new year or prior to the commencement of the holy retreat (*pravāraṇā*), [the merit is especially great].
Regarding the seven-day period: one must establish a separate hall for dhyāna meditation outside the *maṇḍala* site.

After scattering flowers each day, lead all practitioners back into the hall to practice mindfulness by counting the breaths (*ānāpānasmṛti*). If time is short, simply perform the contemplation of counting the breaths before the Dharma seat;
this too should be adjusted according to the circumstances of the moment. Furthermore, this applies both when entering the *maṇḍala* site and when departing from the repentance ritual.

Thus it is. Furthermore, one may recite the sūtras within this hall. What was previously mentioned regarding the recitation of sūtras within the *daochang* (place of practice) was merely to demonstrate the practical application of daily conduct.
Should there be diligent and eminent practitioners who aspire to the ancients and seek realization through the three periods of time as prescribed, no good could be greater.
If one follows the sūtra texts, which apply to all four assemblies, then for those among the assembly of nuns...
The women shall all remain outside the meditation hall of the *dōjō*, single-mindedly making vows and practicing while setting aside all external conditions.
Moreover, since this is fundamentally a *dōjō* for Zen contemplation, all other forms of ritual repentance (*raigyō*) are merely expedient means.

If, however, arrogance is not eliminated, faith has not yet been awakened, and the three karmas are indolent, you will confuse and disturb the assembly; the sages and worthies will not rejoice, and the deities will not grant their protection. Exert yourselves!
Contemplate this.
This is the *Brief Ritual for Cultivation and Realization* of the *Maṇḍala of Perfect Enlightenment*,
composed on the first day of the eighth month in the year of Jihyou (1069 CE), the second year of the Xining era, at the Qinglong Baoge Monastery.
Re-edited on the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of winter in that year.

The *biqiu* (bhikṣu) Baibiao of Pujing Temple on Xi Creek, Shen Jian, respectfully donates his surplus wealth to carve one set of printing blocks for the *Yuánjué xiūzhèng chàn* (Repentance for Cultivating and Realizing the Perfect Enlightenment).
By means of this merit, he reverently offers it to repay the Dharma of his Preceptor of Ordination.
The kindness of the mother’s milk and the merit of the toil of one’s birth-giving parents— next, I pray that all beings throughout the vast nine realms and the four modes of birth,
though deluded, may together ride upon the text of the five repentances and fully realize the profundity of the ten bodies.
At Byakun-ji on Tenshō-zan, the attendant (Jūdō) of the disciples of the ancestral teachings of Master Xianshou,
Sōrei, at the age of seventy-four in the sixth, seventh, or ninth year of Kōan, at Kōmyō-in,
wiped his eyes and transcribed only one fascicle of the *Daśamukha-śāstra*.
Copied on the seventh day of the third lunar month in the second year of the Zhengsheng era at Hōkan-ji Temple in the Imperial Prince’s Sacred Footprint at Yasaka.
This is the postscript to the printed edition of the *Yuanjue jing lüben xiuzheng yi* (The Ritual for Cultivation and Realization Based on the Abridged Version of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment).
Chan Master Guifeng composed the *Yuanjue jing daochang xiuzheng yi* (The Ritual for Cultivation and Realization of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*) in eighteen fascicles.
Although it covers cultivation and realization within a three-period limit, its text is extensive and its meaning is complex, making it inconvenient for those of later learning.
Now, Dharma Master Jinshui has abridged that extensive version into a single fascicle; this work serves not only as a guide for cultivation and realization within a three-period limit, but also...

To practice the ritual of repentance for a single session during the final age of the Semblance Dharma and thereby benefit those who are deluded and confused—this is the humble intention of this compiler.
I have long sought this book, and by chance, I obtained it at Kungang Ryulsa Temple beneath Gubong Peak.
My joy and exultation are beyond compare. Thereupon, the temple master, the Vinaya Master Zhao Rong, took charge of carving and editing this biography to propagate it.

Whether from nearby villages or distant lands, those who rely upon this to practice and realize the truth shall all enter the Great Treasury of Radiance together. Is this not a source of great fortune?
In the third month of the eighth year of the Genroku era (the year of Yi-hai),
during the first ten days of the lunar month, written by Hye-hwang at the Seonggu Bongamgongjeongsa Hermitage.
